Confidence Interval for the Population Root Mean Square Error of Approximation

Source: R/ci_rmsea.R
ci_rmsea.Rd

Constructs a confidence interval for the population root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), a population badness-of-fit index for structural equation models, from a reported RMSEA, its degrees of freedom, and the sample size. The interval is obtained by inverting the noncentral chi square distribution of the test statistic \(T = a\hat{F}\), where \(\hat{F}\) is the minimized fit function and \(a\) the sample size multiplier, and mapping the resulting noncentrality limits to the RMSEA metric (Steiger & Lind, 1980; Browne & Cudeck, 1993).

Usage

ci_rmsea(
  rmsea,
  df,
  N,
  conf_level = 0.9,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  sample_size_convention = c("N-1", "N")
)

Arguments

rmsea

Observed root mean square error of approximation

df

Degrees of freedom of the model, greater than 0 (a model with zero degrees of freedom is saturated, and its RMSEA is undefined)

N

Sample size: greater than 1 under the default sample_size_convention, and greater than 0 under "N"

conf_level

Desired confidence level, between 0 and 1. The default, 0.90, gives the conventional interval for the RMSEA, whose two limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 (see Details).

alpha_lower

The Type I error rate for the lower tail

alpha_upper

The Type I error rate for the upper tail. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound.

sample_size_convention

The multiplier \(a\) with which the reported RMSEA was computed: "N-1" (the default), so \(a = N - 1\), the convention of Browne and Cudeck (1993), of Kelley and Lai (2011), and of ss_aipe_rmsea; or "N", so \(a = N\), the convention of lavaan's default normal likelihood and of Mplus.

Value

A 3-row data.frame with columns term and value. The term values are "ci_lower" (the lower bound of the confidence interval on the population RMSEA, truncated at zero by definition), "rmsea" (the observed point estimate), and "ci_upper" (the upper bound).

Details

The RMSEA expresses the badness of model fit per degree of freedom on the noncentrality scale. Under the noncentral chi square model for the sample fit statistic, \(T = a\hat{F}\) has approximate noncentral chi square distribution with \(df\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter \(\lambda = a \cdot df \cdot \mathrm{RMSEA}^2\). The function rebuilds \(T = a \cdot df \cdot \mathrm{RMSEA}^2 + df\) from the reported RMSEA, obtains the interval for \(\lambda\) by inverting the noncentral chi square distribution at the requested confidence level (ci_nc_chisq does the inversion), and maps its limits back to the RMSEA scale as \(\sqrt{\lambda / (a \cdot df)}\). When the lower noncentrality limit hits zero (i.e., the data are compatible with a well-fitting model), the lower RMSEA limit is truncated at zero because RMSEA is nonnegative by construction.

The multiplier must be the one with which the RMSEA was computed. An RMSEA from lavaan under its default likelihood was computed with \(N\); given to the default "N-1", it gives an interval that matches neither convention, off by an amount of order \(1/N\). Two further cases need the model's chi square statistic rather than its RMSEA, and sem_fit_measures takes it: an RMSEA truncated at zero, which cannot distinguish the statistics below \(df\) that produce it, and the RMSEA of a multiple group model, which carries the factor \(\sqrt{G}\) for \(G\) groups (Steiger, 1998); this function assumes a single group.

The 90 percent CI (rather than the usual 95 percent) is the conventional reporting choice for the RMSEA, from the .05 and .95 percentile points of Steiger and Lind (1980) through Browne and Cudeck (1993), because a \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\) percent interval decides the two one-sided tests at level \(\alpha\), so that the limits of the 90 percent interval settle them at level .05 (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136 and Table 1): the hypothesis of close fit, \(H_0: \mathrm{RMSEA} \le \epsilon_0\), is rejected when the lower limit exceeds \(\epsilon_0\), and the hypothesis of not close fit, \(H_0: \mathrm{RMSEA} \ge \epsilon_0\), is rejected, so that fit within \(\epsilon_0\) is supported, when the upper limit falls below \(\epsilon_0\). A lower limit of zero likewise says that the test of exact fit does not reject at .05. ci_rmsea therefore defaults to conf_level = 0.90, as every RMSEA interval in DMAR does. conf_level = 0.95, the level of the package's other intervals, gives the 95 percent interval, whose limits decide the one-sided tests at .025. The printed table states the level beneath it. See equivalence_rmsea for the test of not close fit with its p-value and verdict.

References

Browne, M. W., & Cudeck, R. (1993). Alternative ways of assessing model fit. In K. A. Bollen & J. S. Long (Eds.), Testing structural equation models (pp. 136–162). Sage.

Kelley, K., & Lai, K. (2011). Accuracy in parameter estimation for the root mean square error of approximation: Sample size planning for narrow confidence intervals. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46, 1–32. doi:10.1080/00273171.2011.543027

MacCallum, R. C., Browne, M. W., & Sugawara, H. M. (1996). Power analysis and determination of sample size for covariance structure modeling. Psychological Methods, 1(2), 130–149. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.2.130

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

Steiger, J. H. (1998). A note on multiple sample extensions of the RMSEA fit index. Structural Equation Modeling, 5(4), 411–419. doi:10.1080/10705519809540115

Steiger, J. H., & Lind, J. C. (1980). Statistically-based tests for the number of common factors. Paper presented at the annual Spring meeting of the Psychometric Society, Iowa City, IA.

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# 1. The conventional 90 percent CI on RMSEA, the default. Its upper
#    limit, 0.052, lies just above 0.05, so the test of not close fit at
#    .05 does not reject an RMSEA of 0.05 or more, and fit within 0.05 is
#    not established even though the point estimate sits well below it.
ci_rmsea(rmsea = .035, df = 40, N = 425)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.015
#>  rmsea    0.035
#>  ci_upper 0.052
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# 2. The 95 percent CI is wider.
ci_rmsea(rmsea = .035, df = 40, N = 425, conf_level = .95)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.008
#>  rmsea    0.035
#>  ci_upper 0.055
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. An RMSEA reported by lavaan under its default likelihood, which
#    forms the statistic with N.
ci_rmsea(rmsea = .0921, df = 24, N = 301, sample_size_convention = "N")
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.071
#>  rmsea    0.092
#>  ci_upper 0.114
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# 4. Fewer degrees of freedom and a smaller N: a wider CI.
ci_rmsea(rmsea = .055, df = 10, N = 100)
#> Note: The lower confidence limit of the noncentrality parameter is at its lower bound, so the lower RMSEA limit is set to 0 based on RMSEA's definition.
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.000
#>  rmsea    0.055
#>  ci_upper 0.129
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
